name: Observational and mathematical astronomy in Babylonia
summary: Babylonian scholars kept dated records of the sky from the eighth century BCE and later built arithmetical schemes predicting lunar and planetary events, which Greek astronomers drew on.
description: Scholars at Babylon kept night-by-night records of the Moon, planets, eclipses and weather, known as the Astronomical Diaries; series of eclipse records reach back to the middle of the eighth century BCE and the earliest surviving Diary dates from 652 BCE. From recurrence periods found in these records they predicted eclipses and planetary phenomena, and in the fifth and fourth centuries BCE they developed arithmetical schemes, preserved on tablets from Babylon and Uruk, that computed lunar and planetary positions. Greek astronomers took over Babylonian parameters and methods about the second century BCE.

impact.note: Its methods and parameters passed into Greek and from there into Indian, Islamic and European astronomy (reach 2); calculated prediction of eclipses and planets was a new capability (depth 2); a whole field grew from it (generativity 2, held below the lead's 3 until descent of the zodiac and degree is sourced).

unresolved.note: Date the first evidenced Saros eclipse prediction and the earliest System A or B ephemeris from a source that edits the tablets.
Settle whether the observation programme began under Nabonassar (747 BCE), and whether the Venus observations of Ammisaduqa count as an earlier record of the same kind.
Source the descent of the zodiac, the degree and sexagesimal time units before raising generativity to 3.

research.note: No older body of dated observations used for calculated prediction is known anywhere, and the cited review shows Greek lunar theory resting on Babylonian parameters; the claim that nothing earlier is known is the supervisor's judgement from general knowledge, not a statement in the source.
